title: Two tools, one turn
spec: M03 · parallel calls, and the leash you don't have yet
intro: A two-part question fans out into two tool calls inside a single model turn, then rejoins. Watch the iteration counter — the whole point is that it doesn't go up.

provenance.source: a narrated run of the six orchestration files shipped in M03 Step 2; the toolbox, the tool descriptions, the question and the expected reply are the module's own, the per-iteration log lines are reconstructed (the module's checkpoint tells you to add them)

foot: Run it for real: any tab from Step 2 — The Orchestration Loop, with print(block.name) added inside the loop.

steps.title: One message, two tool requests
narrative: The question is deliberately two questions: "Where's order AC-1042, and do you have blue running shoes?" No single tool answers it. A newcomer expects two turns — ask, answer, ask again, answer again.

That is not what happens. Iteration 1 comes back with two tool requests in the same response — get_order_status and search_products, side by side. Your loop already iterates over every request, so it runs both without knowing anything special happened.

Watch the argument on the second call. The model sent query="blue", not the whole phrase. With this toy substring matcher that is the difference between one hit and zero — "blue running shoes" is not a substring of any product name. Descriptions route the call; the model still has to pick a sane argument.
steps.youDo: Add print(" ", block.name, block.input) inside the tool loop, then run python orchestrate_anthropic.py.
steps.claudeSays: Issues both calls in one response because neither depends on the other's result — nothing about order AC-1042 changes what to search the catalogue for.

views.text: The saving is one model call here, which is small. It stops being small when a question fans out to five tools — and the latency saving is larger than the token saving, because the two lookups happen at the same time instead of in sequence.

steps.title: Both results, one turn — the #1 bug
narrative: Now the return leg, and the mistake that quietly kills parallelism. The model asked for two things; you must give back both results together, in a single turn, before the next model call.

Split them across two turns and one of two things happens: the SDK rejects the conversation outright, or — worse, because it looks like it works — the model notices the pattern and stops issuing parallel calls at all. Your agent gets slower and you never see an error.

Each SDK spells "both together" differently: one user message carrying two tool_result blocks; one tool Content carrying two functionResponse parts; two function_call_output items appended back to back. Same rule, three envelopes.
steps.youDo: Deliberately break it: messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [results[0]]}) and drop the second. Then put it back.

views.text: The silent version of this bug is the dangerous one. On the SDKs that tolerate it, nothing errors — the model just quietly reverts to one tool per turn, and your agent gets slower for reasons no log explains.

steps.title: Taking the wheel — auto, any, one, none
narrative: By default the model decides freely. Sometimes you want to decide for it, and all three SDKs expose the same four modes behind three different parameter names.

auto is the default and almost always right. required (Anthropic and Gemini call it any) forces at least one tool call — useful when you know the turn is a lookup and a chatty non-answer would be a bug. A specific tool pins one function by name, which turns the model into a deterministic extractor. none forbids tools entirely for a plain-text turn.

There is a fifth switch worth knowing: you can turn parallelism off. Anthropic takes "disable_parallel_tool_use": true inside tool_choice; OpenAI takes parallel_tool_calls=False. Gemini has no equivalent flag — you steer it with the prompt and the mode. Reach for it when your tools share state and running them at once would race.
steps.youDo: Set tool_choice={"type": "any"} and ask a question no tool can answer — "what are your opening hours?" — then watch it call a tool anyway.

views.text: any is the mode people reach for too early. It does not make the model smarter about which tool to pick — it just removes its ability to say "none of these apply", which is often the correct answer. Force a tool only when a text-only reply would genuinely be a bug.

steps.title: The call that should worry you
narrative: One of these three tools is not like the others. get_order_status and search_products read. process_refund writes — it moves money — and right now it sits in the same list, described the same way, dispatched through the same table.

Say the magic words and it fires. Notice what does not happen: no confirmation, no second pair of eyes, no server-side check that this customer is entitled to a refund on this order. A persuasive sentence is the entire authorisation mechanism.

That is the honest limit of this module. The dispatch table that made three tools as easy as one made the dangerous tool as easy as the safe ones. The fix is not a better description — it is human-in-the-loop confirmation and server-side validation before execution, which is the M06–M07 work. For now, the habit worth building is noticing which of your tools are writes.
steps.youDo: Run the refund question and read the loop: find the exact line where the money moves.

before.title: THE TOOLBOX — sorted by what it can break

view.text: The loop did not grow when the toolbox did — three tools, thirty tools, same twelve lines and a dispatch table. That property is exactly why the frameworks in M06–M07 can automate it, and it is the reason the three SDKs converge harder here than anywhere else in the course. But it cuts both ways: the thing that makes tools trivially composable also makes them trivially equal, and a refund is not equal to a lookup. Split your dispatch table by risk before you ship, not after.
